title: "Log Loss"
description: "A probabilistic classification loss that penalizes incorrect predictions more when they are made with high confidence."
term: "Log Loss"
letter: "L"

difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

Log loss measures how well a classifier's predicted probabilities match the
correct labels. It penalizes a confident wrong prediction more heavily than
an uncertain one.

## Technical explanation

For binary labels $y_i \in \{0,1\}$ and predicted probabilities $p_i$ for the
positive class, the average binary log loss is:

$$
-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[y_i \log(p_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right]
$$

For multiple classes, the loss is the negative log-probability assigned to
the true class, averaged across examples. Implementations typically clip
probabilities near 0 and 1 to avoid taking the logarithm of zero.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Log loss evaluates probability quality, not just whether the top predicted
class is correct. It is also a common training objective for probabilistic
classifiers, including logistic regression and neural-network classifiers.

## How it works

Each example contributes the negative logarithm of the probability assigned
to its true outcome. Assigning high probability to the correct class gives a
small loss; assigning very low probability gives a large loss. The total is
usually averaged over the dataset.

## Practical example

Suppose two models both classify an image as "penguin" correctly. One assigns
probability 0.55 and the other 0.99. Log loss rewards the second model's
stronger correct confidence. If that 0.99 prediction were wrong, however, its
penalty would be much larger.

## Common misconceptions

- Log loss is not accuracy: two classifiers can have the same accuracy and different probability quality.
- A lower log loss is better, but only when comparing predictions on a suitable, consistently prepared evaluation set.
- Log loss does not by itself show whether probabilities are well calibrated across subgroups.
